text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- "Brain gymnastics" based on neuro-linguistic programming helps elementary school children concentrate in experiment.
- Finland considers tighter restrictions on fireworks -- products with over 40 grammes of explosives may be prohibited after accidents in the New Year's holiday, officials say.

- Finland's supreme court made its first ruling in which European Union directives took precedence over Finnish law. A Porvoo shopping centre won a value-added-tax deduction which would not be possible according to Finnish law.
- Two army officers fined by supreme court for smelling of alcohol on duty, though they were not apparently intoxicated.
- Forest industry targets lower wood prices in the first round of company-by-company talks with forest owners on purchasing agreements.
KAUPPALEHTI
- New requirements on navigation equipment to cost 150 million markka over three years for national carrier Finnair.
- Northern Finland's forestry entrepeneurs and sawmills say new forest protection programme may put them out of business.
- Large Finnish exporters' finance directors warn that the economy is still vulnerable; the biggest risks this year are export demand and economic policy.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Opposition leader and Centre Party chairman Esko Aho wants the next government after elections in 1999 to be a coalition between his party and the Social Democrats, now the main government party.
- The world's largest paper machine -- UPM-Kymmene's new coated printed paper machine in Rauma which has annual capacity of 400,000 tonnes -- is run by only 96 workers.
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET
- City of Helsinki's electricity utility cut prices by about seven percent at the turn of the year as competition tightens.

- British travel agencies say tours to Lapland featuring Santa Claus and snow safaris are overpriced and commercialised, and the local Sami people feel exploited. But visitors find a seven-hour visit to Lapland money well spent.
DEMARI
- Job-sharing experiments to be expanded to 20 municipalities as employees show increasing interest.
-- Roland Moller, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 242
